pr_body:
Fixes https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/101763
Fixes https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/102393. Tests updates pending.

This change will make queries that don't need any fields from the `_field_caps` call to actually ask only for `_index` field, instead of asking all of them. This will make the `_field_caps` call itself much lighter and its response size almost inexistent (it contains only the list of indices and `_index`).

issue_context.title: ESQL: unexpected count(*) query planning slowdown at scale
issue_context.body:
A simple query like 

```
FROM logs-* 
| STATS count=count(*) 
| SORT count DESC 
| LIMIT 0
```

takes a few milliseconds to execute on a small cluster (< 10 nodes), but on bigger clusters (20 - 70 nodes) it takes hundreds of milliseconds (recorded execution time up to 600ms on a 70 node cluster).

The query is optimized as follows:

```
Limit[10000[INTEGER]]                                                             ! LocalRelation[[count{r}#284],EMPTY]
\_Limit[0[INTEGER]]                                                               ! 
  \_OrderBy[[Order[count{r}#284,DESC,FIRST]]]                                     ! 
    \_Aggregate[[],[COUNT(*[KEYWORD]) AS count]]                                  ! 
      \_EsRelation[person][@timestamp{f}#286, boolean{f}#287, !dense_vector, !..] ! 

```
That seems correct. 

Probably most of the cost is on the planning itself (maybe `_field_caps`?)

Interestingly, adding groupings to the STATS makes things better, eg. a query like

```
FROM logs-* 
| STATS count=count(*) BY agent.version 
| SORT count DESC 
| LIMIT 20
```

is more efficient, and adding one more grouping

```
FROM logs-* 
| STATS count=count(*) BY agent.version, agent.type 
| SORT count DESC 
| LIMIT 20
```

makes it even more efficient.
comments: Yes, the difference lies in the requested fields within the field-caps of these requests. The IndexResolver would request all fields (`*`) for the query `FROM logs-* | STATS count=count() | SORT count DESC | LIMIT 0`, whereas it would only request [`agent.version`, `agent.version`] for the query `FROM logs-* | STATS count=count(*) BY agent.version | SORT count DESC | LIMIT 20`.

The challenge here is to recognize a local relation (aka `limit 0` query) and not create a `*` `_field_caps` call unnecessarily.
Note, though, a `limit 0` query can still need the `*` `_field_caps` call only to be able to return a list of columns with no rows of course. This is not the case for `FROM logs-* | STATS count=count(*) | SORT count DESC | LIMIT 0` (which only needs columns from `stats`) but it is for `FROM logs* | limit 0`.

review_comments:
nit: I guess this has to be in sync with what we do in `preAnalyzeIndices`. Is there maybe a way to refactor this and/or `preAnalyzeIndices` to enforce this (maybe by calling into the same helper function or so)? Specifically, it may be important that we use the same validity verifier, field updater and allowed metadata as in `EsqlSession`.

Otherwise, future changes to `preAnalyzeIndices` might accidentally not lead to test failures here.

There's no easy way to do this kind of testing and, also, keeping it light.
The logic in `preAnalyzeIndices` calls in logic from `IndexResolver` which, in turn is creating a `field_caps` request (and possibly other requests related to aliases and CCS) that goes to ES. The call here is a simplified one where the field_caps response is emulated. What if the field_caps response format changes? This test will not protect us from this.

There is a balance here: test very thoroughly and create IT tests that use the exact code from `preAnalyzeIndices` or isolate the needed logic and do unit tests. I looked into IT tests because of the field_caps output I needed, but I decided it's too much and used unit tests instead. Also, there is another problem with the IT tests: they do not actually look at how the field_caps response look like and how the Analyzer is behaving in that case; the only thing you could assert on is the outcome of a query. OR create more elaborate mocking tests that allows you to run a `field_caps` call as close to reality as possible and then stop the ESQL logic at the analyzer level and look how the analysis is performed. Imo, it's too much work and resources for not so much gain.
Why do we not allow `INDEX_METADATA_FIELD` here, in contrast to the other tests?
Because I don't think it matters for the test itself.
nit: maybe `INDEX_METADATA_FIELD_SET`? i found it a bit confusing when returning a `..._FIELD` for a return of type `Set`.

Everything related to these field names do not have a `set` in their variable names, even if they use `Set` everywhere. And I don't think it should have Set in their name. I regard the Set as an implementation detail to help eliminating duplicates. If I change this to `...._SET` I'd want to change everything related to field names to something ending in `Set` (in IndexResolver, EsqlSession and tests as well). I think it's clear enough like it is now.

super nit: if possible, I think it'd be a tad cleaner to return an empty set here and then check for emptiness when calling `fieldnames`; mapping "no field names found" to "let's just use `_index`" sounds like the (pre-) analyzer's job, and I'd rather expect `fieldnames` to just return what fieldnames it finds in the plan.

So, there are three situations here:
- just a regular list of fields extracted from the plan. Like `from test | keep first_name`
- all fields, simply because they are needed: `from test`
- and no fields at all because we don't need to read anything from Lucene `from test | stats count(*)`
`fieldNames()` job is to decide what `_field_caps` will use in its call.
On one hand  having all this logic in this static method helps greatly with unit testing.
On the other hand, there is logic outside `fieldNames` that changes its content already, like fields needed for enrich policies.

I'll have another look at this. For unit testing's sake, I think I will integrate the enrich policies default match fields logic inside `fieldNames` and add some more tests to `IndexResolverFieldNamesTests`.
To clarify, this minor remark is meant as highly optional. Nice-to-have if `fieldnames`'s responsibility vs. `preAnalyzeIndices` would be super clear, but not worth putting in real effort IMO :)

I've reworked this. Mostly because of how enrich policies were handled, and it turned out there was a small improvement there. Thanks for raising the discussion point. Even though I haven't addressed your exact concern, something was definitely improved there.
